doc.title: Nick Brignola interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 28, 1997

title: Italian saxophonists from Upstate New York
summary: They note upstate Italian players like Monterose, Nistico, Noto and Menza, and he says they rarely hung together.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: You know there’s been, I guess we can consider you an Upstate New York guy, all the way from Albany to Buffalo, and there’s been really quite a long list of great jazz players to come out of —

Usually like from the center of the state, you know, J.R. Monterose, Sal Nistico, the Mangione brothers and then on the west side we had like Don Menza and Sam Noto. But I think I’m the only one from Albany.
You know I just noticed a weird thing as you went through those names is they all end in a vowel.
Yeah, they all happen to be Italian.
I don’t know. They often used to say that, you know like all these Italian saxophone players. I don’t know. I think it’s just coincidence. On the other hand, I don’t know.

I don’t know. They talk about the Texas Tenors, you know, and a certain sound indicative of certain areas. I never really heard those guys until I’d already been playing. I mean I knew Chuck Mangione and Sal, and I knew J.R. But I didn’t meet Sammy Noto until I’d been playing maybe ten, fifteen years, and I don’t ever remember meeting Don Menza — and I’m sure I’m leaving out some guys, I’m sure there’s some other great players around. But we never really hung together. I mean I was from Albany and I just, I never saw these guys. Once in a while they would come to Albany, like J.R., when I first met J.R. he came to Albany to play a gig and I found out he was from Utica, but I didn’t hang out with him that much. You know in later years we hung out, but as far as influencing each other, I don’t know. But there was a certain flair I guess that always people said that the Italian tenor players from Upstate New York. So I’ll go along with perpetuating that myth.
